source.title: On the Entropy Calibration of Language Models
source.authors: Steven Cao; G. Valiant; Percy Liang

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses language-model scaling laws and uses a similar log-scale fitting approach, but its empirical target is entropy calibration error, not held-out pretraining loss, compute-optimal allocation, or the other listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The empirical scaling results measure the gap between generation entropy and log loss on human text as model size changes. They do not report held-out pretraining loss scaling or test whether the listed loss-scaling versions hold. The paper also reports temperature and instruction-tuning tradeoffs, but those do not test the listed versions.
record.test_reason: The paper fits log entropy-calibration error (generation entropy minus log loss on human text) against log model size for existing Qwen2.5, Llama 2/3 and Pythia base models. It borrows the log-log fitting method from Kaplan et al. and Hoffmann et al., but reports no fit of held-out pretraining loss against parameters, tokens or compute. It also reports no compute-optimal allocation, shape comparison, extrapolation test or downstream-task scaling. Calibration error is a related but different construct, so it goes under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. More precisely, the authors find that entropy miscalibration improves very slowly with model size on text (exponents near 0) and moderately on code (about -0.3), in line with the data's power-law tails. Temperature reduction and instruction tuning both reduce entropy at the cost of higher log loss. They prove that a future-entropy adjustment could in principle calibrate without raising log loss, given a black-box regression fitter.
record.recipe_differences: Measures generated-text entropy calibration error against model size rather than held-out pretraining loss against parameters, tokens, or compute; also develops a theoretical calibration procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Calibration-error scaling exponents differ by dataset and model-family cohort; the authors speculate that changes in training data mixtures and midtraining may contribute, but note that controlled data mixtures are needed to disentangle effects.

fits_no_version.finding: Log calibration error versus log model size fits a line. Exponents are about 0 (older families) or about -0.13 (newer families) on the two text datasets, and about -0.2 / -0.35 on CodeContests.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Entropy calibration error of base LMs follows a power law in model size. Its exponent depends on the data's tail heaviness and on the model family, and is near zero for text.

fits_no_version.finding: In a stylized unigram power-law setting, expected singleton mass scales as m^(1/alpha-1), which is very slow when alpha is near 1.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Rare-item mass, a proxy for generation derailment, declines slowly with training sample size under Zipfian data.

record.problems: The empirical scaling study covers three datasets and reports no uncertainty for the fitted exponents. Training details for three of the four model families are not public, and the authors say model size, dataset size, and dataset composition are not disentangled. They also state that more datasets and controlled data mixtures are needed.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant reported results were left out. The paper's temperature and instruction-tuning comparisons concern calibration-diversity tradeoffs rather than the listed scaling-law versions.

untested.parts: No fit of held-out loss against parameters, tokens or compute. Per-model log loss is plotted in Fig. 2 but not fitted against size.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
No fixed-compute allocation between parameters and tokens.
No architecture-shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
No loss scaling in other modalities or training regimes.
No downstream-task performance fitted against scale or loss. Calibration error is not a downstream task metric.
Exponents vary by dataset and model cohort only for calibration error, not for pretraining loss or the compute-optimal split.

record.verdict_notes: All rows correctly carry versions ["none"]. Their 'observed' states describe the calibration-error fits themselves, not any claim version. Model size is confounded with data size and data mix (the authors note this), and no uncertainty is given for the exponents. The paper is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not test held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameter count, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fits are used to predict losses of larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation between parameters and tokens is evaluated.
The paper does not compare architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No cross-modal or alternative-training-regime test of the stated loss-scaling form is reported.
The paper does not test downstream-task performance scaling or its predictability from pretraining loss.

Scaling exponents vary by dataset and model-family cohort for entropy calibration error, but the paper does not test fit dependence or curve bending for held-out pretraining loss or compute-optimal allocation.
